Title: Judging Criteria for the European Championship 2003 (advice needed)

Messages.Author: Damnans
Messages.Body:
These are the judging criteria we have been working on
until now.

Any help to improve them or to add more of them to the list
will be appreciated :)

JUDGING CRITERIA FOR THE EUROPEAN CHAMPIONSHIP: BARCELONA 2003

Judges will be as strict as fair. The V:EKN Judges' Guidelines
will be implemented according to the following criteria:

ILLEGAL DECKS: Decks will be inspected at random during the 3
preliminary rounds of both the Spanish Qualifier and the European
Championship. And all of the finalists' decks will be inspected
before the start of the final. If a player's deck is proven
illegal after the third round has finished (before the start
of the final), and the appropriate penalty for the infraction
in the V:EKN Judges Guidelines is a game loss, judges will
disqualify that player instead. The next highest ranked player
in the tournament will then take his or her place in the final
round.

DEALS INVOLVING VICTORY POINTS: Although these deals are
perfectly legal, players must know that judges will tend to
disapprove of such deals unless there is a powerful reason
supporting them. For this reason, before any player makes a deal
of this kind, the involved players must report that deal to a
judge; the judge will determine if the deal is legal or not.
This rule is not meant to penalize players making winning deals
(i.e., deals giving them the game win), but to keep a close eye
to those players making losing deals (i.e., deals not giving them
the game win) when they actually have real chances to get more
victory points by not making such deals.

SELF-OUSTS: Self-ousts of any kind should also be reported to a
judge in advance. Unless the chance for a player to get more
victory points is zero, judges will not allow that player to oust
him or herself.

OFFICIAL LANGUAGE: Unless each player at a given table speaks
the same language, each player will have to speak English during
their games. In the case that there are players who don't speak
English, they sould call a judge as a translator.

IDLE PLAYERS: Players who have already finished their games will
have to leave the room where games of the current round are still
running.

Thanks in advance for your help.

Greetings,
Damnans

Bear in mind that we have a judge who "disapproves" of legal play and
requires "powerful" reasons to convince him that I should, in fact, be
able to play legally. If I'm not gifted at "powerful" explanations of
why I should be able to do something that is entirely legal, will I even
bother to suggest it? I know it's legal, but I'm very easily tongue-
tied *especially* in a situation where I could be speaking in a foreign
language. I couldn't do "powerful" if I tried, because my English is
limited or unexpressive relative to what I *know*. Or just that the two
of us are crap at explaining ourselves, even when both fluent, but we
both know what we want do and can both see that it's in our mutual
interests. But it's still legal (or illegal), whether I can explain it
or not. Deals don't suddenly become more legal when I become better at
being powerful, or more illegal because I can't.

A legal deal is a legal deal, whether I can explain my reasons
powerfully to a judge who disapproves or not.

Impeding legal play with warnings of disapproval and the need to explain
yourself powerfully are counter-productive to finding a European
Champion. The idea is find the best player. The best player is the one
who can play the game best. The game consists of many legal plays and
play styles and situations - including some which might want to be
looked at for future revisions, but are part of the game *now*. Biasing
a tournament against certain forms of legal play stops it being a
tournament to find the best player, but the best player who can play
under not-quite-the-actual-rules.

Why anyone should want to prejudice a tournament in this fashion is
beyond me.

First of all, the word you are looking for is "collusion". This would
normally not matter. However, "coalition" is a term which could easily
refer to entirely legal deals. A "coalition government" is one where
two parties form an alliance in order to gain a majority to pass
mutually beneficial legislation, for instance. So the term "coalition"
is unfortunately confusing here.

Second of all, you need to understand what the collusion rules are
about.

Collusion is:

Players agree to alter, predetermine, or otherwise illegally
establish the results of a game.

However, this needs to be clarified, of course. Any discussion
(potentially) alters the results of the game in some fashion.

Hence:

* No player introduces incentives outside the current game such as
cash, cards, or other items.
* No part of the agreement has been secret or has taken place
outside of the current game.
* No part of the agreement involves a random selection of the
winner.
* The agreement does not otherwise violate section 5.2 of the V:EKN
Tournament Rules.

In a situation along the lines of the one you present, neither player is
offering bribes, cards or whatever. No part of the agreement is secret,
as far as we can tell. There is no random selection. 5.2 refers to
Unsportsmanlike Conduct - which this *could* be. But that's a separate
offence to collusion and there is no need to bring collusion in. An
illegal deal is an illegal deal, collusion or no. And collusion is
*HARD* to prove with any satisfaction.

Why do I say this *could* be Unsportsmanlike Conduct? One simple reason
is that two decks could know full well they're about to mutually
annihilate each other. It is *not* collusion to rely on previously
known information. For instance, if you know that someone is playing a
Turbo-Wynn deck and so are you, there could be grounds for some sort of
agreement taking place. I could contest you and screw up your game. It
would be unusual, but two such decks could have knowledge that the other
one is playing - perhaps, in a small tournament[0], they faced each
other in an earlier round. Or you bring out Wynn and I discuss with you
that I'm about to bring him out too, and so we talk and come to some
arrangement.

A similar situation could have occurred (but didn't) at the European
qualifiers run here last week - four Salubri decks in one tournament.
Very horrible.

You *can't* rule against previous knowledge, it's simply not possible in
any meaningful fashion. And previous knowledge does not mean collusion.
It's collusion when playing for an external goal, not when playing with
external knowledge which, let's face it, everyone gathers over time.
(Like "Rob Treasure will play Dramatic Upheaval at some point".)
However, early deals *can* mean Unsportsmanlike Conduct, but don't
necessarily have to in extreme cases.

[0] Remember that in an under 20 tournament, only a 16 player tournament
(4 lots of 4) can sufficiently mix up the tables so that you never see
anyone again.

I don't know what you really mean, but thanks to the help of other
constructive members of this newsgroup, I have made some modifications
to the Judging Criteria for the EC, which stay as follows:

JUDGING CRITERIA FOR THE EUEOPEAN CHAMPIONSHIP

Judges will be as strict as fair. The V:EKN Judges' Guidelines will be
implemented according to the following criteria:

THE GOAL OF THE GAME (REMINDER):

Players must play to win.

- If one has multiple paths to victory, then one is free to choose from
among those paths.
- If one cannot win, then one is obliged to maximize one's Victory Points.
- If there are multiple paths available to achieve the most Victory Points

one can get, then one is free to choose.

- If one cannot win, and the most Victory Points one can acquire is "0 more
than currently acquired", then one is free to acquire those 0 more Victory
Points in any manner one wishes.

ILLEGAL DECKS: Decks will be inspected at random during the 3 preliminary
rounds of both the Spanish Qualifier and the European Championship. And all
of the finalists' decks will be inspected before the start of the final.
If a player's deck is proven illegal after the third round has finished
(before the start of the final), and the appropriate penalty for the infraction
in the V:EKN Judges Guidelines is a game loss, judges will disqualify that
player instead. The next highest ranked player in the tournament will then
take his or her place in the final round.

DEALS INVOLVING VICTORY POINTS: Although these deals are perfectly legal,

players must know that judges will disapprove of such deals unless there is
a factual reason supporting them. For this reason, before any player makes a

deal of this kind, the involved players must report that deal to a judge; the
judge will determine if the deal is legal or not. This rule is not meant to
penalize players making winning deals (i.e., deals giving them the game win),
but to keep a close eye to those players making losing deals (i.e., deals not
giving them the game win) when they actually have real chances to get more
victory points by not making such deals.

SELF-OUSTS: Self-ousts of any kind should also be reported to a judge in
advance.
Unless the chance for a player to get more victory points is zero, judges will
not
allow that player to oust him or herself.

WITHDRAWALS: Note that a player has the option to withdraw from the game ONLY if
he or she has exhausted his or her library and begins his or her turn with less
than a full hand. Players who want to withdraw from a game and do not meet those
requirements will have to discard all of their cards in a legal manner before
announcing their withdrawal.

OFFICIAL LANGUAGE: Unless each player at a given table speaks the same language,
each player will have to speak English during their games. In the case that
there
are players who don't speak English, they sould call a judge as a translator.

IDLE PLAYERS: Players who have already finished their games will have to leave
the
room where games of the current round are still running.

Greetings,
Damnans

Having to get details secondhand allows for either outright lying, or
the "chinese whispers" problem where information gets distorted in the
transmission. (i'm sure everyone's played the game where you stand in a
circle, whisper a nonsense phrase to the person to your left, and so on,
and when it comes back to you it doesn't even remotely resemble what you
said?)

With regards to a previous post about "what if the player is making a
deal with the intent to break it?"...

If the player is making a legal deal, then the judge doesn't have to
pull anyone aside or change his ruling, and the treachery can continue
unabated.

If the player is making an ILLEGAL deal that can only become legal if
broken, then it should immediately be obvious to everyone at the table
that such a deal can only be legal if not kept, and therefore is not
really a deal at all. No need for the judge to pull anyone aside here
either; he simply rules the deal illegal. It doesn't matter how you
arrange for a judge to pull someone aside, as soon as he does anything
but speak to all the players in public, it should be an instinctive
reaction to flag the deal as "will be broken".

-- Derek

things like the Continental Championships and the regional
qualifiers. Because it can be fun to play some "serious"
VTES games once in a while. But this can only work well
when everyone involved in the games is willing and able to
play in the spirit of trying to win and not being a jerk or
a dork about the game.

Deals that give someone else the game win are mostly bullshit.
You know that's my opinion. The only reason I can see that
people are willing to take second place in games is that the
tournament environment raises the stakes to the point that it
can be worth getting second place so you get more prizes or
a chance at making it to the finals or whatever. In a "normal"
game of VTES, second place just means you're one of the people
that didn't win. (I know that some people are willing to throw
games even in pickup, but it's an alien concept to me. I guess
second place is better than fifth, but not enough to be worth
throwing in the towel and conceding that first is impossible.)

In other words, to me, it's tournament VTES that distorts the
"ideal" version of the game. Helping someone else win is
borderline unsportsmanlike at best and is never fun or cool.

> LET THE PLAYERS PLAY.

>
> LET THE PLAYERS PLAY.

It's a cute slogan, Kevin, but I don't think it is in any
way a useful approach to judging. Players make mistakes
*all the time*. I rarely see a game of VTES where no one
misplays even a single card or rule. I've even been known
to do it myself, and I'll bet you have too. :-) Players
can't figure out everything for themselves: they don't know
the rules that intimately and they can make mistakes even
if they do. And that's assuming that nobody's *trying* to
cheat. (Which of course we *hope* will be the case, but it's
probably ridiculously optimistic to assume that it never will
be.)

Josh

Um, your counter-argument isn't really one. My evidence is this: At finals I
judge, and other finals I watch, I have observed that sometimes people talk out
loud as they choose where they sit. Particularly the top three seeds, who
actually have some control. In fact, it seems like 99% of all people think out
loud as to where they will sit. Some 5% of those perhaps are dissembling to
some degree, but that's not really material to our discussion, except
tangentially. Anyway, as I listen to these people discuss their decision as to
where they will sit at the table, they often mention their other finals
opponent's deck styles as a *key* factor in how they will sit in opposition or
ally with them. Perhaps not the only factor, but a key factor. So I have
observed that knowledge of deck type is a key factor in a person's decision on
where to sit. This may not actually help them win, but it might.

In VTES, where you sit at the table has a huge huge impact on how your game will
go. Again, it's not the only factor, but I think we can all agree that it is a
major factor in how you and your deck will fare. At tournament finals, this is
one of the rare times when the participants of a particular game of VTES can
have some modicum of control over where they will sit, with knowledge of what
some of the other decks at the table will be. When we sit down to a casual,
first of all, the seating is usually randomly determined. Secondly, unless one
of our opponents only owns one deck, we have no idea what deck they are going to
bust out on us. But at a tournament final, we have an opportunity to know what
decks will be there in the final, and if we are 1st, 2nd, or 3rd seed, we can
control somewhat the environment of that final for our decks.

Granted, it is not out of the question that one person can get to the final and
have played every other deck there, and another gets there and has not played
any of the other decks there. Well, that is part of the random nature of the
seating draw in the preliminary rounds, and is definitely part of the overall
tournament structure. However, simply either being a victim of or user of a
fast deck that sweeps should not give you an advantage over your opponents in
the finals. That is my contention.

Now, as I was putting these thoughts down, I thought of one method perhaps to
counter scouting. I could announce at the beginning of the tournament that all
finalists will be required to give a brief (10 words or less) description of
their decks prior to anyone choosing seating. This way, all finalists will have
at least some knowledge of what they will be seating against. How about that
fix? Then scouting might not be any issue at all.

he determines that it is a losing deal (regardless of the intentions
of the players), then he can rule that the player can only make the
deal if he intends to break it.

> So, does the judge just assume that every deal is entered into with
> the intention of honoring it (and judge accordingly)?

No.
Deals can be made with the intention to break. In that case, however,
there is no repreive from the "play to win" rule when it comes to
potentially honoring the deal.
If a deal is made such that the honoring is legal, then it can be
honored even if, when the time comes to pay the piper, the play to
win rule would dictate otherwise.
